notes: Human feedback for the MHM learning layer.
Use this for taste, placement and organization signals after reviewing the live map.
This file should stay factual and music-related. Do not add albums or songs as node targets.

feedbackCategories.label: Too dense
feedbackCategories.feedback: A local cluster is too compressed. Nodes may sit close together, but labels must remain readable and important names must not stack.

feedbackCategories.label: Label overlap
feedbackCategories.feedback: Visible labels collide or form unreadable piles. The renderer should hide lower-priority labels when zoomed out, and layout should increase spacing.

feedbackCategories.label: Wrong zone
feedbackCategories.feedback: A node is placed in a zone that does not match its strongest music-history context.

feedbackCategories.label: Good bridge
feedbackCategories.feedback: A node usefully connects two or more zones. Preserve its cross-zone pull instead of forcing it into a sealed cluster.

feedbackCategories.label: Bad node type
feedbackCategories.feedback: A candidate is not one of the allowed visible map node types: band, guitarist, artist, guitar, guitar_brand or genre.

feedbackCategories.label: Genre transition needed
feedbackCategories.feedback: Neighboring scenes need more documented bridge nodes so the map reads like a music-history flow, not separate boxes.

feedbackCategories.label: Category grouping
feedbackCategories.feedback: Category-like labels such as duos, groups, people, artists, albums or companies are not concrete music genres and should not become visible nodes.

feedbackCategories.label: Platform or reference
feedbackCategories.feedback: Music platforms, magazines, databases, institutions and reference works are source context, not visible map nodes.

bridgePolicies.feedback: Gospel, blues and swing feed R&B; R&B and gospel feed soul and early rock. Preserve the distinct traditions and let only documented anchors create cross-zone pull.
Western swing combines country dance music with jazz and blues; Bakersfield inherits selected elements. Keep the country center legible while these documented anchors lean outward.
The rock to hard-rock/metal path should overlap strongly. Let bridge nodes drift between zones rather than forming a straight, sterile lane.
Punk should connect back into rock history while keeping its own chaotic identity.
Hip-hop should keep a readable territory while allowing documented crossover lines into punk, rock and metal.
Give jazz its own readable center. Let documented blues, fusion, funk and progressive connections pull bridge nodes outward.
Keep early country, bluegrass and honky-tonk legible as a tradition, with documented paths into folk, blues, rockabilly and rock.

The Yardbirds' documented membership links three guitarists to different later directions. Keep the shared band history visible without implying the three played in the band at the same time or followed one identical style.
Luther Perkins' documented Esquire use behind Johnny Cash connects a specific guitar to early country. Cash is context, not the player.
Johnny Marr's documented Jaguar design gives a specific guitar-to-player link. The model's hardware specifications alone do not establish a genre connection.
George Harrison's documented use on Beatles recordings is a player-to-instrument bridge. Do not treat a later purchase inspired by the Beatles as a shared performance.
Steve Vai's documented JEM design links a guitarist to a model. Keep instrument design distinct from teacher and band relationships.
Jazz fusion is a transition, not a sealed genre island. Preserve jazz as the center and let documented electric guitar, rock and funk relationships form its outward paths.

nodeFeedback.feedback: Keep gospel a distinct sacred tradition. Its documented influence on R&B and soul is a historical bridge, not evidence that the genres are interchangeable.
R&B is the junction of documented blues, gospel and swing influences and later soul/rock developments. Do not collapse it into any one source.
Birth of the Cool is a specific Davis-led jazz phase. Keep it within jazz and distinct from his later modal and electric phases.
Modal jazz describes an improvisational approach, not a claim that all Davis or Coltrane recordings use modes.
Place western swing in country roots while letting its documented jazz, blues and big-band ingredients explain cross-zone connections.
Keep Bakersfield with country. Its honky-tonk, western swing and rockabilly ingredients explain the louder regional sound without turning it into generic rock.
Outlaw country is partly about control over material, studios and musicians. Do not infer that all outlaw artists share one fixed musical style.
Charles is a documented bridge: gospel phrasing entered R&B and soul, and he also recorded country. Keep influence, genre and repertoire links distinct.
Franklin's gospel upbringing and R&B recordings explain her soul and pop connections; a gospel influence is not the same as a later secular genre label.
Wills anchors western swing in country while his documented jazz and blues ingredients justify outward connections.
Owens anchors Bakersfield; R&B is documented dance-hall repertoire, not a reason to reclassify him as an R&B artist.
Jennings's Outlaw placement rests on documented recording autonomy and work with Willie Nelson, not on a generic rebellious visual label.
Keep Rodgers grounded in early country while letting his blues and early rock influence pull him toward those scenes.
The Carter Family is an early country anchor with documented folk and blues repertoire.
Haggard belongs in country while his documented jazz and blues influences make him a useful bridge.

nodeFeedback.label: Misfits
nodeFeedback.feedback: Core punk and horror punk anchor. Keep near Ramones, Sex Pistols, horror punk and hardcore punk rather than generic rock.

nodeFeedback.label: Ramones
nodeFeedback.feedback: Major early punk anchor. Should help organize the punk-alt area and connect back to rock history.

nodeFeedback.label: Sex Pistols
nodeFeedback.feedback: Major UK punk anchor. Should sit in the punk-alt core with clear relation to Ramones and early punk.

nodeFeedback.label: Black Sabbath
nodeFeedback.feedback: Should behave as a bridge between hard rock, doom metal and heavy metal rather than sitting in a closed metal box.

nodeFeedback.label: Led Zeppelin
nodeFeedback.feedback: Important overlap point between blues rock, classic rock and hard rock.

nodeFeedback.label: Public Enemy
nodeFeedback.feedback: Hip-hop anchor with possible punk/rock crossover context. Keep hip-hop in its own area, but allow documented bridges.
Keep the band in British blues rock. Clapton, Beck and Page are documented former members whose later paths explain its wide bridge role; membership does not imply a shared later sound.
Connect the Yardbirds and Cream through verified membership, with blues guitar as the musical center. Hall of Fame inductions are career context, not new collaborations.
The Yardbirds are the documented roots link; later instrumental work gives Beck a separate jazz-fusion direction. Keep those reasons distinct.
Page links the Yardbirds' blues-rock lineage to Led Zeppelin's hard rock. His double-neck guitar is a separate instrument-use link, not a genre by itself.
Keep jazz fusion attached to jazz while allowing documented rock, funk and progressive crossover. Do not pull every nearby jazz artist into rock.
Teaching, band work and guitar design are three different relationship types. Keep Vai close to Satriani, Zappa and the JEM for their documented reasons, not as one generic collaboration cluster.
The documented Vai link is teacher-to-student. Keep it distinct from a shared recording or band-membership edge.
The model belongs with Fender guitar history. Its documented use by Luther Perkins behind Johnny Cash gives it a specific country bridge; do not infer that Cash himself played this model.
The Harrison/Beatles recording use supports a concrete instrument-to-player bridge. A later artist being inspired to buy the model is influence context, not proof of a shared recording.
The genre name's link to Bill Monroe's band is an origin clue. Keep bluegrass rooted in early country and acoustic folk history, not modern pop-country.
A funk sample or stylistic debt explains musical lineage. Keep G-funk in hip-hop; do not treat every funk influence as a direct artist-to-artist collaboration.

factFeedback.interpretation: This records a Hall of Fame induction, not a joint performance or musical collaboration. Do not create a collaboration edge from it.
Use as evidence for separate membership links and a British blues-rock lineage. Do not infer simultaneous membership.
Satriani taught Vai; Zappa later employed him. These are teaching and band/career relationships, not interchangeable collaboration edges.
This supports Page's use of a double-neck on stage. It explains an instrument connection, not a new musical genre.
A pickup-switch specification enriches the guitar node only. Do not derive an artist or genre edge from hardware alone.
The player was Luther Perkins, backing Johnny Cash. Keep Cash as scene context; do not claim Cash played the Esquire.
A documented player and recording context can bridge instrument and band. The guitar model remains in the workshop zone.
This is a genre-origin relationship, not a claim that one person alone invented every part of the style.
Use as a stylistic and production lineage inside hip-hop. Funk influence is not by itself a documented collaboration with a specific funk artist.
The band's sound experiments support a stylistic bridge into psychedelia. Keep this separate from its member-to-member links.

zoneFeedback.feedback: Jazz needs a readable center and historically supported transitions. Keep early jazz and jazz guitar together while allowing fusion and crossover artists to drift toward rock and prog.
Prioritize early country history. Keep this area spacious and let well-sourced country, folk, blues and rockabilly bridges cross its boundary.

Rock is the connective tissue. It should overlap with roots/blues, hard rock/metal, prog/psychedelia and punk instead of becoming a sealed box. Rock circuit may be dense and messy, but it must never become a crushed cluster. Nodes can sit close together, but labels should remain readable and should not overlap across multiple names. When rock, blues rock and hard rock nodes crowd together, spread them outward and preserve readable lanes between related groups.
Hard rock and metal should be dense, but not isolated. Black Sabbath, Led Zeppelin, Deep Purple, Van Halen, AC/DC and punk/metal crossover nodes should bleed across borders.
Punk/alternative should feel chaotic and connected, not boxed. Let hardcore, horror punk, post-punk and alternative scenes cluster, but allow cross-zone drift.
Hip-hop needs its own readable territory while still allowing documented crossover lines into funk, punk, rock and metal.

rules.feedback: Zones are guidance, not cages. Strong bridge nodes may bleed outside the visual rectangle when it improves readability.
Wikipedia categories are weak signals. Do not create or prioritize category-like genre nodes unless they are recognized music genres.
Songs, albums and releases can explain a connection, but should not become graph nodes.

Never allow the map to become visually unreadable. Dense clusters are acceptable when they feel like organized chaos, but labels must not overlap heavily, node labels must remain readable, and important names should not stack on top of each other. If a zone becomes too crowded, expand the local layout, increase spacing, or let bridge nodes drift outward instead of compressing everything into one tight cluster.
